claims.text: There is a blog post titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ that provides a closer look at the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
There is an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
There are upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code is essentially a code generator that produces an intermediary format such as YAML or JSON, which is then executed to deploy resources.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, instead of generating an intermediary format.
AWS CDK supports only AWS as a cloud provider, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers real-time debugging.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as languages, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK has slower deployment speed due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers faster direct execution.
AWS CDK has poor visibility making it hard to trace errors, while Pulumi provides clear deployment state.
AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem, while Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows.
AWS CDK state management relies on a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi offers cross-cloud secret support.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as programming languages.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, whose constructs (components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform, with potential supplemental income from enterprise services and consulting.
SST's transition from CDK to Pulumi is empowering developers with a more flexible, provider-agnostic approach to infrastructure management.
Moving from AWS CDK to Pulumi unlocks multi-cloud flexibility, faster deployments, and a better developer experience for SST.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.

SST's Founding Engineer is quoted saying: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'

The CDK/CloudFormation approach starkly contrasts with Pulumi because the intermediary CloudFormation templates often obscured underlying logic and made it more difficult to diagnose and resolve problems.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running SST's `sst deploy` requires no Pulumi account.
Nitric runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
Defang runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
SST's public team attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account.
This post covers where SST stands 'as of this writing' / 'in 2026', implying the facts about SST's release and download numbers are current as of the article's publication date.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
SST's team began a rewrite code-named Ion in late 2023 that replaced its entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
SST v3 (Ion) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped in mid-2024.

SST wrote in its blog post "Moving away from CDK": "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST wrote in its blog post "Moving away from CDK": "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST's docs page "What is SST" states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin wrote in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis": "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka wrote in "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion": "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `package.json` for SST's platform package lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST's deployment chain, `sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state and orders operations, Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls, and state is written to an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than Pulumi Cloud.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools without a Pulumi account, the same way Pulumi's engine embeds for SST.
Pulumi's Terraform provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric's own docs state: "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Nitric's official providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket, not in Pulumi's hosted service, and SST does not require a Pulumi account to work.
Because SST's constructs/components compile to Pulumi resources, resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
SST's latest release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` package on npm is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week as of this writing.
npm download stats for `sst` show 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode.
opencode is an open source AI coding agent that has grown quickly since launch.
opencode now carries a larger following on GitHub than SST itself.
SST's release cadence and download numbers indicate SST is not being abandoned despite the team's broadened public attention.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state.
Pulumi's policy as code feature lets a platform team enforce guardrails centrally.
Pulumi's components feature allows sharing infrastructure patterns across a whole organization rather than just within one SST app.
SST v3 (the Ion rewrite) shipped mid-2024.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components are defined using Terraform providers but bridged through the Pulumi engine.

Reaching for Pulumi directly makes more sense once a user needs cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application, since that runs on the same engine SST already uses.
The linked post "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK, from SST's side.
The GitHub star count for `anomalyco/opencode` was observed in September 2026.
The SST repository was formerly named `sst/sst` and is now `anomalyco/sst`.
